summary.zh: 卡茲科普寓言（庫辛自其母舍夸所聞）：小獴至正分剖其群所射大羚之狐獴處，與之爭獲而不果——此屬螳螂神話之系列。

title.en: The Anteater's Laws: The Springbok, the Lynx and the Partridge
title.zh: 食蟻獸之法：羚、獰貓與鷓鴣

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §33

summary.en: The anteater inquires of each springbok ewe whether her child is female; a foolish ewe confesses, the anteater springs into a hole with the kid, and lays down the law about the proper food and proper marriages of every animal. The lynx repeats her words, and later steals the daughter back, unlooses her bowstring on the anteater's head, and becomes the springbok-eating lynx, marrying a lynx.
summary.zh: 食蟻獸逐一詢問母羚其子性別；愚母吐實，食蟻獸攜羔入穴，並立萬獸飲食與婚配之法。獰貓復述其言，後又盜回其女，解弓弦於食蟻獸之首，遂成食羚之獰貓，並娶獰貓為妻。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth-fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§33): the Anteater inquires from a flock of springbok ewes, one after another, whether her child is a female. Each mother answers that hers is a male, until, at last, a foolish springbok confesses that her child is a daughter. The anteater offers to hold the child, so that the springbok should eat some of the anteater's food. The latter then springs into a hole with the kid.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §33; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The male springbok scolds his wife for having lost their child. The anteater then lays down the law with regard to the proper food for different animals, and that their marriages should be suitable. They all listen to the anteater, and also to the lynx, who repeats to them the anteater's words... in the directions given about marriage, some animals marry wives, others husbands — a trace, Bleek notes, of a former grammatical gender in Bushman.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §33; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In another version the daughter of the springbok, \khauko, is stolen away by the lynx, who marries her. The anteater, told of this by the partridge, follows them underneath the ground; whereupon the lynx unlooses his bowstring and throws it down, the anteater's head is caught in it, and the lynx orders her to become altogether an anteater and live in a hole. Then he takes back the young springbok to her mother, becomes the lynx who eats springbok, and marries a lynx.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §33; not verbatim.

summary.en: The quagga, who fed her hungry child with a piece of her own liver, died by her husband's doing: the jackal put poisoned pieces of sharp bone into her bed because his relations said that he had married 'meat'. Her death was avenged by her own family.
summary.zh: 母斑馬以己肝一片哺飢兒；死於夫手：豺因親屬譏其娶「肉」為妻，置毒骨碎屑於其褥。其死由母族復仇。

title.en: Sho-loii: The Medicine of the Snakes

region.zh: 奧蘭治河山區（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§107-108

summary.en: Sho-loii, a Bushman vegetable medicine and charm, grows in the mountains near the Orange River; men fight after rubbing their hands with it and heal each other after. An ignorant digger of sho-loii was found speechless among serpents; a skilled application drove the snakes away — taking the harmful scent with them — and restored him.
summary.zh: 紹洛伊為桑人草木藥與符，生於奧蘭治河近山；鬥者先以此擦手，戰後再以之互醫。一無知掘者被發現無言僵坐群蛇之中；善用此藥者驅蛇——連其惡嗅同去——並救醒之。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San medicine-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§107): \slo-loii, a Bushman vegetable medicine, used also as a charm (L II.—36. 3242-3261). How one man fights with another, having previously rubbed his own hands with \slo-loii; and how he afterwards restores the man with whom he fought by means of a fresh application. The sho-loii in general use is not found upon the flats, but in the mountains near the Orange River; when dug out, the Bushmen replant part of it with a small piece of the root.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §107; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus (§108): an ignorant man having gone to dig up sho-loii is discovered speechless and motionless, sitting among serpents, by the hole where he had been digging. By a skilful application the snakes are driven away, taking with them the scent which had injured the man, and the man is restored to speech and motion.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §108; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dying Man's Last Speech and the Widow's Lament

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §112

summary.en: Wounded by a companion's arrow while hunting springbok, a man begs that they speak gently, not angrily, to the shooter — for unlucky shots come from the remissness of wives, children playing on beds; he gives his widow advice, and she cries that she would like to cry herself to death and will not eat, and will not marry again for fear of a lesser husband.
summary.zh: 獵羚時為同伴之箭所傷，其人求眾人對射者溫言勿怒——因失準之射乃由婦人怠慢、孩童戲床所致。他留遺言於寡妻；妻泣欲哭至死、不食、不再嫁——恐遇不及故夫之良人。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San death-narrative from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§112): a man is accidentally wounded by another, when they were both hunting springbok. Dialogue, in which the wounded man begs them to speak gently, not angrily, to the one who shot him. Unfortunate shots are believed to be due to such causes as the children at home playing on a man's bed, etc., and are ascribed to the remissness of the wives.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §112; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The dying man's last speech to his wife, in which he gives her advice. The widow's lament, in which she says that she should like to cry herself to death, and does not want to eat food; her mother-in-law comforts her. After the burial the widow returns home to her father, where her brothers receive her very well; she expresses her intention not to marry again, for fear of meeting with a husband who had not the good qualities of the deceased.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §112; not verbatim.

title.en: The Hyena Defends Her Gemsbok from the Lion

summary.en: The hyena, defending from a lion the game (a gemsbok) which she is carrying home for her children, bites his thigh, so that he retires in pain — told by !A!kunta from the personal experience of his maternal grandfather \kui-\go, who was still living when his grandson left Bushmanland.

summary.en: The Knorhaan (Brandkop bustard) who married his sister — told to Dia!kwain by his mother; apparently a version of the fable embedded in the Anteater's Laws, in which the bustard's head was thrust into the fire for the incestuous marriage.
summary.zh: 娶其妹之冠鴇——戴亞寬自其母所聞；似為食蟻獸之法中所嵌寓言之一版：因近親婚配，其首被按入火中。
